subtype: Hands behind the back in respect [Expressing]
passage: I work two desks from Yusuf, so I saw the whole thing. When the regional head walked into our Pune office, Yusuf stopped mid-sentence and stood with his hands clasped behind his back, chin level, listening. I am Reena, and I thought it looked very formal, almost stiff. The regional head asked him about the delivery figures and Yusuf answered clearly, still standing that way. Later in the canteen, Yusuf stood with his hands in his pockets like anyone else, joking with the driver. I cannot tell whether the earlier pose came from respect or nerves. He told me he grew up standing like that before elders at school assemblies.

qa.a: They most likely showed respect and attentiveness toward the regional head, which he confirmed with his school habit. Reena also wondered if it was nerves, so it could also have been stiffness.

qa.q: What does Yusuf's relaxed stance in the canteen suggest?
qa.a: It suggests the formal pose is tied to setting and the presence of a senior, so it is not his general way of standing.

qa.q: How might the regional head have taken Yusuf's posture?
qa.a: The regional head probably saw it as respectful and attentive, though a person from a more casual office could find it stiff.

subtype: Hands behind the back in respect [Expressing]
passage: Sabina, you asked why I still stand with my hands behind my back when the director walks in. I'm Lokesh, and I've done it since I was a trainee in the Madurai mill office. My first supervisor stood that way before the owner, so I did too. It meant: I'm listening, I respect you. Then, at twenty-five, I went for training in Rotterdam. First day, the engineer in charge, a tall woman called Ms. Visser, looked at me standing there like a soldier and laughed kindly. "You look like you're waiting to be scolded. Sit, relax." I felt so awkward. In her office, hands behind the back looked stiff and nervous, not respectful. So I learned to keep my hands loose, or hold a notebook. When I came home, I went back to the old way. Same respect, different shape.

qa.q: Where did Lokesh go for training at twenty-five?
qa.a: To Rotterdam.

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel when Ms. Visser laughed and said to relax?
qa.a: Lokesh felt awkward and a little embarrassed, since the posture meant respect at home but looked stiff and nervous to her; her laugh seemed kind rather than mocking.

qa.q: What choice did Lokesh make in Rotterdam, and why did it work?
qa.a: Lokesh kept the hands loose or held a notebook, matching the local style so the respect came across without looking stiff.

qa.q: How did Ms. Visser read the hands-behind-the-back stance?
qa.a: She saw someone waiting to be scolded, stiff and nervous, and wanted to put the trainee at ease.

grounding: An elder recalls standing with hands behind the back as respect at home and learning it looked stiff in another country's workplace.

subtype: Hands behind the back in respect [Expressing]
passage: The interview room at the Guwahati office had a drilling crew right outside the window, so every answer had to be said twice. When Arohi was called in, she stood by the chair with her hands clasped behind her back, the way she had always stood before teachers and elders. Two panelists nodded approvingly. The third, Yamini, who had spent ten years at a firm in Toronto, frowned slightly. "Please sit. You look very stiff," she said over the drilling. Arohi's cheeks warmed. Was that a bad sign? She sat, then said, "Sorry, in my family, standing like that is how we show respect to seniors." Yamini's face softened. "Ah. Where I worked, it reads like a soldier waiting for orders. Good to know." The drill stopped for a moment. In the sudden quiet, the interview went better than Arohi expected.

qa.q: How many years had Yamini spent at a firm in Toronto?
qa.a: Ten years.

qa.q: How did Arohi feel when Yamini called her stiff?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and worried 😰, wondering if it was a bad sign, since she had meant the stance as respect.

qa.q: What helped clear up the misunderstanding?
qa.a: Arohi briefly explained that standing with hands behind her back shows respect in her family, so Yamini could read it correctly.

qa.q: Why might Yamini have read the stance differently from the other two panelists?
qa.a: After ten years in Toronto, where it looks like a soldier waiting for orders, Yamini saw stiffness, while the other two recognised a familiar respectful stance.

grounding: Shows a young professional standing with hands behind the back to show respect before seniors and one interviewer reading it as stiff.

subtype: Hands behind the back in respect [Expressing]
passage: At the Chembur music academy's annual concert, Pallavi was on usher duty near the green room. When Simran-ji, the old sitar teacher, came down the corridor on a student's arm, Pallavi stepped aside and stood straight, hands clasped behind her back, head slightly lowered. Simran-ji paused, looked at her and smiled. "You were my student's student, no? Good manners." Pallavi felt a small glow. A few minutes later, a little boy waiting with his mother tugged at Pallavi's dupatta. "Didi, what are you hiding behind your back?" She laughed and showed him both empty hands. "Nothing! It's how I show respect to Simran-ji." The boy looked unconvinced, then put his own hands behind his back, copying her, just as the first notes of the evening began.

qa.q: Where was Pallavi on usher duty?
qa.a: Near the green room at the Chembur music academy's annual concert.

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel when Simran-ji praised her manners?
qa.a: Pallavi felt a small glow of pride and warmth, pleased that the stance was read as the respect she meant.

qa.q: How did Pallavi handle the boy's question well?
qa.a: She laughed, showed her empty hands and explained simply that it was her way of showing respect, clearing up his confusion.

qa.q: How did the little boy read Pallavi's hands behind her back?
qa.a: He thought she might be hiding something, which shows the same stance can look secretive to someone who doesn't know the custom.

grounding: Shows a young adult standing with hands behind the back before a respected senior, read as good manners by one person and as hiding something by a child.

subtype: Hands behind the back in respect [Expressing]
passage:
"Why were you standing like a school monitor in front of the director?" Payal asked as they walked back to their desks.
"Like what?"
Payal clasped her hands behind her back and straightened up. "Like this. Chin up. For ten whole minutes."
Vidya laughed. "Oh. Habit. At my convent school we stood like that for the principal. Hands behind, no fidgeting. It meant, I'm listening, I respect you."
"It's sweet. But the director asked you twice to sit, and you kept standing. She looked a bit uneasy."
"Really?" Vidya's smile slipped. "I thought she'd take it as respect."
"She might. In my last office in Singapore, one manager hated it; said it felt like a military inspection."
"So what do I do? Just flop into the chair?"
"No. When a senior asks you to sit, sit. Keep the respect in how you listen."

qa.q: Where did Vidya learn to stand with her hands behind her back?
qa.a: At her convent school, where they stood like that for the principal.

qa.q: How did Vidya feel when Payal said the director looked uneasy?
qa.a: Vidya felt surprised and a little embarrassed, because the posture was meant as respect and attention. 😅

qa.q: What would you advise Vidya for next time?
qa.a: Sit when a senior invites her to, and show respect through attentive listening rather than a rigid stance.

qa.q: How might the director have seen Vidya's stance?
qa.a: The director may have read it as respectful, or as stiff and overly formal, which could explain looking uneasy when her offer to sit was ignored.

grounding: Hands behind the back before a senior can mean respect and attention, but in another setting it can seem stiff.
